title: Grow, remember, and trust what we saw
sum: Peter greets readers who were given "a faith just as precious as ours" and sets out what God has given: everything needed for life and godliness, and promises by which they may become "sharers in the divine nature" (1:4). God's gift calls for effort, and a ladder of eight qualities climbs from faith to love (1:5–7). Those who climb it make their calling firm and will be welcomed into Christ's eternal kingdom.

Then the letter turns into a farewell. Peter knows his "tent" will soon be laid aside, as Jesus showed him, and he wants them to remember. He answers a charge that the apostles followed "clever myths": they were eyewitnesses on the holy mountain when the Father's voice honored Jesus. The prophetic word is a lamp until day dawns, and it came not by human will but from people "borne along by the Holy Spirit" (1:21).
readings: The chapter has the shape of a famous person's last words: his death is near (1:14), he wants his teaching remembered after his "departure" (1:15), and in the next chapter he foretells false teachers. Whether Peter wrote it himself or a later writer used the form in his name, the form tells readers how to hear it: this is the apostle's lasting legacy, meant for the church after him.
Read as Christian ethics in Greek dress

Divine power, divine nature, godliness, goodness, self-control: the chapter speaks the language of Greek moral philosophy. But the gifts come from Christ, the goal is his kingdom, and the ladder begins with faith and ends with love. The chapter claims that what the best of the Greek world hoped for is given in Christ, and must be lived out.

views.H: Readers in a Greek-speaking world (most think Asia Minor, if 3:1 refers to 1 Peter) hear a farewell from the apostle, set against teachers who called the apostles' message of Christ's coming a fable. The transfiguration is offered as eyewitness proof of the glory to come.
views.C: For most critical scholars, the testament form, the Greek religious vocabulary and the defense of apostolic witness point to a writer after Peter's death, using Peter's name and memory (see the book's opening pages). Defenders of Peter as the writer point to the personal memory of the mountain and the word of Jesus about his death.
views.L: Notice the chain of 1:5–7, where each virtue grows inside the last, and the repeated words: "supply" (1:5, 11), "eager" (1:5, 10, 15), "remind" (1:12, 13, 15), and "carried" or "borne" (1:17, 18, 21). The voice was carried from heaven, and the prophets were carried by the Spirit: both come from God.
views.J: The chapter draws on Israel's prophets and on the Jewish farewell testament (Jacob, Moses, the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs). The "star" of Numbers 24:17 may lie behind the morning star of 1:19, and the voice on the mountain echoes Psalm 2:7 and Isaiah 42:1. Peter's Hebrew name, Simeon, opens the letter.
views.T: 1:4 is the classic text for theosis in the Orthodox Church, and the Catholic Catechism cites it (460); Calvin and Wesley read it more cautiously, and Lutherans are divided. 1:20–21 is a key text on inspiration and on who interprets Scripture. See the two cards below.

deep.h: A ladder from faith to love (1:5–7)
deep.b: The eight qualities are linked like a chain, each one supplied "in" the one before: faith, goodness, knowledge, self-control, endurance, godliness, brotherly love, love. Six of the eight are words Greek moralists used. The frame is Christian: faith at the bottom (the gift received, 1:1) and love at the top. The ladder is not a way to earn salvation; it starts from what God "has made us a gift of" (1:3–4). But it is not optional either: without these qualities a believer is "blind" and forgetful (1:9), and with them he "will never trip" (1:10).

Verses 12–15 are the heart of the letter's claim to be Peter's last word. Those who think Peter wrote it read a real memory: Jesus had shown him how he would die (John 21:18–19), and he wants his teaching kept after he is gone. Those who think a later writer used Peter's name read the testament form, well known in Jewish writing, as the means by which a follower passed on what he believed Peter would say to a new generation. Richard Bauckham argued that such a testament would have been understood as a recognized form, and that "the pseudepigraphal device is therefore not a fraudulent means of claiming apostolic authority" (in his Word Biblical Commentary, as quoted by Ray Van Neste). Others, such as Michael Kruger, see no reason to doubt the letter's own claim. The book's opening pages set out both cases.

deep.title: Claude's theory: three words from the mountain
deep.b: This is my own suggestion. In 1:13–18 the writer uses three words that belong to the transfiguration story: "tent" (skēnōma, 1:13–14; Peter offered to build tents on the mountain, Matthew 17:4), "departure" (exodos, 1:15; Moses and Elijah spoke of Jesus' "exodus," Luke 9:31), and "glory" (1:17). I think the cluster is deliberate: Peter, who once wanted to pitch tents and stay on the mountain, now speaks calmly of folding up his own tent and making his own exodus, as his Lord did. Commentators note the individual echoes; reading the three as a designed sequence that turns Peter's mistake on the mountain into his readiness for death is my own reading.

echoes: Acts 15:14; Titus 2:13; 1 Peter 1:2; Jude 2; Romans 5:3–5; Galatians 5:22–23; John 21:18–19; 2 Corinthians 5:1–4; Luke 9:31; Matthew 17:1–8; Mark 9:2–8; Luke 9:28–36; Psalms 2:7; Isaiah 42:1; Numbers 24:17; Revelation 22:16; 2 Timothy 3:16; Jeremiah 23:16

settings.by: "Simeon Peter, a slave and apostle of Jesus Christ"
settings.to: "those who were given a faith just as precious as ours": believers who never saw Jesus, most likely Gentile churches in Asia Minor if 3:1 refers to 1 Peter
settings.when: at the opening of a letter written as Peter's last word
settings.why: The greeting gives the readers equal standing with the apostles: their faith is of the same value, a gift received from "our God and Savior, Jesus Christ." That matters for readers being told by new teachers that the apostles' message was a myth. The wish that grace and peace grow "in the knowledge of God" sets the theme: true knowledge of Christ, against a counterfeit.

settings.what: What God has given, and the ladder of growth
settings.by: Peter, as the letter presents him
settings.to: the same readers, who, the letter says, had been cleansed from their old sins (1:9), and are now tempted to drift
settings.when: before the warnings, as the foundation for them
settings.why: Before he warns, Peter reminds them of what they already have: everything for life and godliness, and promises that make them sharers in God's nature. Then he calls them to effort, with a list of virtues that Greek-speaking readers would recognize from their own moral teachers. Knowing the readers explains the vocabulary: Peter speaks their language to say that the good life they admired is God's gift in Christ and leads to his eternal kingdom.

settings.what: Peter's farewell and his defense of the apostles' witness
settings.to: the readers, who will live on after him and will face teachers who call the apostles' message "clever myths"
settings.when: as Peter expects to die soon, as Jesus showed him
settings.why: The farewell gives the letter its authority and its purpose: to be remembered after Peter's "departure." He answers the charge of myth with eyewitness testimony from the holy mountain, and with the prophetic word, which came from God. For the first readers this anchored their hope in Christ's coming to two sure things: what the apostles saw and what the prophets spoke.
views: Peter writes shortly before his death, perhaps through a helper (defended by Michael Green and Michael Kruger).

A follower writes after Peter's death, probably late in the first century, in the recognized form of a farewell testament, to pass on Peter's teaching to a later generation facing new teachers (Richard Bauckham and most critical scholars).

settings.what: The Father's voice on the holy mountain
settings.to: Jesus, in the hearing of Peter (with James and John, as the Gospels tell it) on the mountain
settings.when: at the transfiguration, during Jesus' ministry
settings.why: The voice declares Jesus to be God's dearly loved Son and gives him "honor and glory." Peter cites it as proof that the glory of Christ's coming is no myth: he heard the voice himself. For the letter's readers the scene is a preview of the power and coming they are waiting for (1:16).

traditions.q: What does it mean to become "sharers in the divine nature" (1:4)?
views: This is salvation itself: theosis, being made by grace a sharer in God's life without becoming God by nature. Vladimir Lossky wrote that union with God "in His energies" is "union by grace making us participate in the divine nature," and that "in deification we are by grace (that is to say, in the divine energies) all that God is by nature." Athanasius: "He was made man that we might be made God" (On the Incarnation 54).

The Catechism quotes 2 Peter 1:4 when it explains why the Word became flesh: "to make us 'partakers of the divine nature'" (Catechism 460), citing Irenaeus, Athanasius and Thomas Aquinas, and it describes grace as making believers "partakers of the divine nature and of eternal life" (Catechism 1996).

Lutherans are divided. The Finnish school of Luther research (Tuomo Mannermaa and others) argues that for Luther, Christ is really present in faith and "faith divinizes the one doing the believing," close to the Orthodox teaching. The Formula of Concord rejects the view that the righteousness of faith is "God's essential righteousness" dwelling in us, and teaches that God's indwelling "follows the preceding righteousness of faith, which is nothing else than the forgiveness of sins" (Solid Declaration 3).

Calvin wrote that "the word nature is not here essence but quality": believers do not become part of God's being, a view he rejected, but the gospel aims "to render us eventually conformable to God, and, if we may so speak, to deify us."
Wesley read it as renewal in God's image and communion with God: "Being renewed in the image of God, and having communion with them, so as to dwell in God and God in you."

traditions.q: Does "no prophecy of Scripture comes into being by a person's own interpretation" (1:20) say who may interpret Scripture?
views: The Second Vatican Council cites 2 Peter 1:19–20, with 3:15–16, for the inspiration of Scripture (Dei Verbum 11). On interpreting it, the Council teaches that Scripture "must be read and interpreted in the sacred spirit in which it was written," that "the living tradition of the whole Church must be taken into account," and that the interpretation of Scripture "is subject finally to the judgment of the Church" (Dei Verbum 12), whose "living teaching office" alone has the task of "authentically interpreting the word of God" (Dei Verbum 10).

The Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem, 1672) says the Scriptures are to be believed "not otherwise than as the Catholic Church has interpreted and delivered the same," since "one and the same Holy Spirit" is "the author of both," and the Church's witness is "not of inferior authority to that of the Divine Scriptures" (Decree 2).

"The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself": a doubtful passage is to be understood by other places "that speak more clearly" (Westminster Confession 1.9, whose proof texts include 2 Peter 1:20–21). The supreme judge in every controversy is "the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture" (1.10).

The prophetic and apostolic Scriptures "alone" are the rule and norm of all teaching; other writings, even the creeds and confessions, "must not be regarded as equal to the Holy Scriptures" and are received only "as witnesses" of how Scripture has been understood (Formula of Concord, Epitome, "Rule and Norm").

Wesley read the verse as being about where prophecy comes from, not about readers: "It is God, not the prophet himself, who thereby interprets things till then unknown." On 1:21 he added that the prophets "were purely passive therein."

title: False teachers, and a God who rescues and judges
sum: As there were false prophets in Israel, so false teachers will come, sneaking in factions, disowning the Master who bought them, and making money out of the church. Their judgment is not asleep. The proof is in Genesis: God did not spare the angels who sinned, the world of Noah's day, or Sodom and Gomorrah, but he guarded Noah and rescued righteous Lot. So "the Lord knows how to pull godly people out of testing" (2:9).

The rest of the chapter is a portrait of the teachers, much of it reworked from Jude 4–16: bold and self-willed, slandering the glorious ones, like animals that cannot think, stains at the church's meals, followers of Balaam who loved the pay for wrongdoing, waterless springs. They promise freedom but are slaves. Those who escaped the world and go back are worse off than before, like the dog and the sow of the proverbs.
readings: Line up this chapter with Jude 4–16 and the borrowing is plain, and so are the changes: 2 Peter drops the books outside Scripture (1 Enoch, the story of Michael and Moses), puts the examples in the order of Genesis, adds Noah and Lot as people God rescued, and makes Jude's present-tense intruders into a prediction that is already coming true. The topic page Jude and 2 Peter sets them side by side.
Read as hope as well as warning

The long sentence of 2:4–9 is not only about judgment. Its goal is 2:9: God knows how to rescue the godly. Noah and Lot were a few among many, distressed by the world around them, and God kept them. Readers surrounded by a lawless culture, and by teachers inside the church, are told that they are not forgotten.

views.H: Traveling teachers depended on the churches' support, and the letter accuses these of greed and of feasting at the church's meals. They seem to have offered new converts from paganism a "freedom" that let them return to their old ways (2:18–19).
views.C: The dependence on Jude weighs heavily in the debate over date and authorship: most scholars hold that 2 Peter used Jude, which would place 2 Peter after Jude. The chapter's shift from future ("there will be") to present ("these people are") is read as a sign that the prediction is a literary device of the testament form.
views.L: The chapter is built on one long "if ... then" sentence (2:4–9), then a string of portraits joined by "these people" (2:12, 17) as in Jude. Wordplays: wronged / wrongdoing (2:13), stains and flaws (2:13, turned around in 3:14), baited (2:14, 18), slaves and freedom (2:19).
views.J: The angels in Tartarus (Genesis 6 as Jewish tradition told it), Noah the preacher (Josephus, the Sibylline Oracles), righteous Lot (Wisdom 10:6), Balaam the prophet for hire, and a proverb from Proverbs 26:11: the chapter reads Israel's Scriptures as Jewish teachers of the time did.
views.T: 2:1 ("the Master who bought them") is a classic text in the debate over whether Christ died for all; 2:20–22 in the debate over whether a true believer can fall away (see the card at Hebrews 6:4–6).

deep.b:
Where the Greek is the same, the Plain uses Jude's wording; where 2 Peter changes the Greek, the Plain changes too. The main differences:

  • Prediction, not report. Jude says intruders "slipped in" (Jude 4); 2 Peter says false teachers "will" come, then speaks of them in the present.
  • No books outside Scripture. Jude quotes 1 Enoch (Jude 14–15) and tells of Michael and the devil (Jude 9). 2 Peter keeps the points but names neither: "angels" do not slander (2:11), and Enoch's prophecy is gone.
  • Genesis order and rescue. Jude's examples are Israel in the desert, the angels, Sodom (Jude 5–7). 2 Peter has the angels, the flood, Sodom, in the order of Genesis, and adds two rescued righteous men, Noah and Lot.
  • Fewer pictures. Jude's clouds, trees, waves and stars (Jude 12–13) become springs and mists (2:17); Cain and Korah (Jude 11) drop out, Balaam stays and gains his donkey.
  • Love feasts and deceptions. Jude's "love feasts" (agapais) and "sunken rocks" (spilades) become "deceptions" (apatais) and "stains" (spiloi), near-twins in Greek.

The letter gives their behavior more than their doctrine. They were teachers inside the church (2:1), greedy (2:3, 14), sexually loose (2:2, 10, 14), contemptuous of authority and of angels (2:10), present at the church's meals (2:13), and they promised "freedom" (2:19). Chapter 3 adds their teaching: Christ will not come, and the world is not under God's judgment (3:4). Readings: (1) Epicurean-style skeptics: Epicureans denied that the gods judge. Jerome Neyrey read the opponents against that background, and Peter Davids follows him (as Ernst Baasland's review of Davids reports); David deSilva says the majority of scholars now place the teachers there. (2) Twisters of Paul: 3:15–16 suggests they used Paul's teaching on grace and freedom. (3) Early Gnostics: an older view, now less common, since the letter says nothing of their typical ideas. The views can be combined.

echoes: Jude 4–16; Deuteronomy 13:1–5; Jeremiah 23:9–32; Matthew 7:15; Genesis 6:1–4; Genesis 6–8; Genesis 19:1–29; Wisdom 10:6; Numbers 22–24; Numbers 31:16; Proverbs 26:11; Matthew 12:43–45; Hebrews 6:4–6; 1 Peter 3:20

settings.by: Peter, speaking in the manner of a farewell prophecy
settings.to: the readers' churches, where such teachers were already at work (2:10–22 speaks of them in the present)
settings.when: after the reminder that true prophecy comes from God (1:19–21)
settings.why: The contrast is deliberate: Israel had true prophets and false ones, and so the church will have true apostles and false teachers. Calling them a fulfilled prediction strips them of surprise and of authority: the apostle saw them coming. For the first readers, the charges of greed and of disowning the Master named the danger in terms they could test.

settings.to: the same readers, some of whom were being told that God does not judge
settings.when: in the argument against the false teachers
settings.why: One long sentence: if God judged the angels, the ancient world and Sodom, and rescued Noah and Lot, then he knows how to rescue the godly and keep the unrighteous for judgment. The examples answer both the teachers' denial of judgment (3:4) and the readers' fear: God sees the few faithful among many.

settings.what: A portrait of the false teachers
settings.to: the readers, so that they can recognize the teachers among them
settings.when: in the main warning of the letter
settings.why: The portrait does not argue with the teachers' ideas; it exposes their lives: their contempt, appetites, greed and empty promises. The point for the first readers was practical. People who promise freedom but are slaves of their cravings are not guides to follow. The final proverbs warn those tempted to go back that the old life is a dog's vomit and a pig's mud.

title: Where is the promise? The day of the Lord
sum: This second letter, Peter says, is a reminder: remember the prophets and the command of the apostles. Mockers will come asking, "Where is the promise of his coming?" They say the world has gone on unchanged since creation. But they forget that God's word once let the world be drowned in water, and the same word keeps the present heavens and earth for fire on the day of judgment.

God is not late: with him a day is like a thousand years, and the delay is his patience, because he wants all to come to repentance. The day of the Lord will come like a thief; the heavens and elements will be dissolved, and the earth and its works will be "found." Believers wait for new heavens and a new earth where righteousness is at home, and they live holy lives meanwhile. The letter ends by naming "our beloved brother Paul," whose letters some twist like "the other Scriptures," and with a call to grow.
readings: Read as a world ending in fire

Many readers, following the KJV's "shall be burned up," have taken 3:10–12 as the annihilation of the material world, replaced by a wholly new one. On this reading the passage stresses how temporary everything is, and how foolish it is to live for it.
Read as a world judged and renewed

Others note that the oldest Greek says the earth and its works "will be found," that the world "came to ruin" in the flood without ceasing to exist, and that "new" can mean renewed. On this reading the fire is a judgment that purges and exposes, and the same creation comes out of it made new (compare Romans 8:19–22).

views.H: The readers were troubled by a delay: Jesus' coming had seemed near, and the first generation ("the fathers") had died. Teachers used the delay to deny that God judges at all. The chapter answers both the doubt and the denial.
views.C: Three details weigh in the debate over date: "the fathers fell asleep" (3:4), "your apostles" (3:2), and Paul's letters as a collection alongside "the other Scriptures" (3:16). Many scholars read them as signs of a writer after the apostolic generation; others give each a reading that fits Peter's lifetime.
views.L: Watch the word "found": in Greek the earth and its works "will be found" (3:10, where the Plain says "will lie exposed"), and believers must be "found by him without stain" (3:14). And the word "promise": the mockers ask where it is (3:4), the Lord is not slow about it (3:9), and believers wait for what he promised (3:13).
views.J: The chapter is built from Jewish Scripture and tradition: creation from water (Genesis 1), the flood, Psalm 90:4 on a thousand years, the day of the Lord as a thief, fire at the judgment (Isaiah 66:15–16; Malachi 4:1), and new heavens and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17; 66:22). Jewish writers such as the author of Jubilees used Psalm 90:4 in the same way.
views.T: 3:9 is cited in the debate over whether God wills the salvation of every person; 3:10–13 in debates over the end of the world; 3:15–16 in the history of the canon and the question of who may interpret Scripture.

deep.h: Burned up, found, or not found? The end of the world in 3:10
deep.b:
The verse's last word decides much of its meaning, and the manuscripts disagree (see the manuscript note). The oldest Greek copies say the earth and its works "will be found." Because that seemed to make no sense, later copies changed it: "will be burned up" (the Byzantine text and the KJV), "will vanish," "will be found dissolved" (Papyrus 72), and, in two early translations, "will not be found." NA28 and the Editio Critica Maior now print that last reading, a conjecture with the negative, although no Greek manuscript has it.

Three readings of the oldest text have defenders:

  • Exposed for judgment. "Found" is courtroom language: everything people have done will be laid open before God, with nowhere to hide (Richard Bauckham's reading, as Al Wolters reports it).
  • Refined. Al Wolters argues that "found" was used for metal recovered after smelting, so the fire purifies the world rather than destroying it.
  • Destroyed and replaced. Readers who follow "burned up" or "not found" see the old world ending and a wholly new one beginning, as "the first heaven and the first earth had gone away" (Revelation 21:1).

The Plain follows the oldest Greek and renders it "will lie exposed." Whatever the last word, the passage plainly says: the day will come without warning, it will bring judgment, God's promise is a new world "where righteousness makes its home," and believers should live now in a way fit for that world.

The mockers' question, "Where is the promise of his coming?" (3:4), was a real problem for early Christians. Jesus had spoken of the end as near (Mark 9:1; Mark 13:30), and the first generation was dying. 2 Peter gives four answers: (1) God has acted in the world before, at the flood, so "nothing changes" is false (3:5–7). (2) God's time is not ours: a day is like a thousand years (3:8). (3) The delay is patience: God wants all to repent (3:9). (4) The day will still come suddenly, like a thief (3:10). Believers may even "hurry it along" by holy living (3:11–12). See the topic page on "Soon" and "Near."

deep.title: Claude's theory: "found" ties the ending together
deep.b: This is my own reading, though it builds on commentators who link 3:10 and 3:14. The verb "find" appears twice in the last chapter: the earth and the works in it "will be found" (3:10, in the Greek; the Plain says "will lie exposed"), and the readers must "be found by him without stain and without flaw, in peace" (3:14). I think the writer chose the hard word in 3:10 so that 3:14 would answer it: on that day everything will be found, so make sure that when you are found, you are clean. If that is right, the oldest reading is not a puzzle to be fixed but the hinge between the description of the end and the call to holy living, and the later copyists who changed it lost the link.

echoes: Jude 17–18; Psalms 42:3; Jeremiah 17:15; Genesis 1:2–10; Genesis 7:11–24; Psalms 90:4; Isaiah 34:4; Isaiah 65:17; Isaiah 66:15–16; Isaiah 66:22; Malachi 4:1; 1 Thessalonians 5:2; Matthew 24:35–44; Romans 2:4; 1 Timothy 2:4; Revelation 21:1; Galatians 2:11–14

settings.what: A reminder, and the mockers' question answered
settings.to: the readers, "beloved," who were hearing the mockers' claim that Christ will not come
settings.when: after the warning about false teachers, as the letter turns to their central teaching
settings.why: Peter quotes the mockers so that the readers can see the claim for what it is, and answers it from Genesis: the world has not always gone on unchanged; God's word once ended it by water and will judge it by fire. For readers whose first leaders had died, it rebuilt confidence that the promise still stands.

settings.by: "mockers" in the last days, people who live by their own desires
settings.why: The saying is meant to make believers give up their hope: no coming, no change, no judgment. Quoting it inside the letter defuses it: the apostles foretold that people would say exactly this (3:3).
views: Nothing has changed since the patriarchs died.
The fathers are the first Christians
Nothing has changed since the first generation of believers died, though Jesus was expected to come in their lifetime. Most scholars take this view.

settings.what: God's time and the day of the Lord
settings.to: "beloved": the faithful readers, not the mockers
settings.when: as the answer to the delay
settings.why: The section turns the delay from a problem into a mercy: God is patient because he wants all to repent. Then it describes the day of the Lord so that the readers will live as people who belong to the new heavens and new earth. The first readers were meant to wait without giving up and without despair.

settings.when: at the end of the letter
settings.why: The ending gathers the letter's threads: be found clean, count the Lord's patience as salvation, agree with "our beloved brother Paul," beware of those who twist his letters, and grow. Naming Paul as a partner told readers who may have heard Paul used by the false teachers that the apostles stood together.
